lessons.title: Dependency Management via package.json & Lockfiles
lessons.description: package.json defines your project's dependencies and scripts — the manifest of any Node.js project.

sections.heading: What is package.json?
paragraphs: Every Node.js project starts with a package.json file. It defines your project name, version, dependencies, scripts, and configuration. It's the control center for your project.
list: npm init — creates a new package.json
dependencies — packages needed in production
devDependencies — packages only needed during development
scripts — custom commands you can run with npm

sections.heading: Lockfiles
list: package-lock.json (npm) — pins exact versions of every dependency
pnpm-lock.yaml (pnpm) — same purpose, different format
Lockfiles ensure everyone on your team uses the same versions
Always commit lockfiles to version control

codeExamples.heading: package.json basics
explanation: scripts define custom commands: npm run dev runs the dev script.
dependencies are production packages — installed with npm install.
The ^ prefix means compatible with the version (allows minor updates).

practice.task: Initialize a new npm project and add a script that logs "Hello" when you run npm run hello.

keyTakeaways: package.json is the manifest for every Node.js project.
Use npm install package-name to add dependencies.
Always commit lockfiles — they ensure consistent installs across environments.
Scripts define reusable commands for your project.
lessons.challenge: Set up a project with express as a dependency and nodemon as a devDependency. Add a dev script that auto-restarts the server.

lessons.title: Semantic Versioning Rules (SemVer)
lessons.description: Version numbers follow MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — understanding them prevents breaking changes.

sections.heading: SemVer explained
paragraphs: Semantic Versioning (SemVer) uses three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Each number has a specific meaning about the type of changes in the release.
list: MAJOR — breaking changes (API incompatible with previous version)
MINOR — new features (backward compatible)
PATCH — bug fixes (backward compatible)
Prefixes: ^ (allow minor), ~ (allow patch only)

codeExamples.heading: SemVer in practice
explanation: No prefix means exact version: 18.2.0 → only 18.2.0.
Lockfiles pin the exact installed version regardless of these ranges.

practice.task: Look at a package-lock.json and identify 3 packages with different version ranges. Explain what updates each range would allow.
hints: Search for ^, ~, and exact versions in the lockfile.

keyTakeaways: Use ^ for safe minor updates and ~ for patch-only updates.
Lockfiles override version ranges with exact installed versions.
Always check a package's changelog before updating major versions.
lessons.challenge: Explain why a lockfile is essential even with version ranges in package.json.

lessons.title: Package Execution: npm, pnpm, bun Performance Differences
lessons.description: Compare package managers — npm, pnpm and bun differ in speed, disk usage and installation strategy.

sections.heading: Package manager comparison
list: npm — the original, most widely used, copies packages to node_modules
pnpm — faster, uses a content-addressable store, saves disk space
bun — fastest, written in Zig, combines runtime and package manager
All three are compatible with package.json and lockfiles

codeExamples.heading: Installing with different managers
codeExamples.code:
# npm
npm install express
npm run dev

# pnpm
pnpm install express
pnpm run dev

# bun
bun install express
bun run dev

# All three read the same package.json
# pnpm and bun are significantly faster than npm
explanation: All three managers use the same package.json format.
pnpm uses symlinks to a central store — saves disk space.
bun is the fastest — combines package management with the runtime.
Choose based on your project needs and team preference.

practice.task: Install the same set of dependencies using npm, pnpm, and bun. Compare the installation speed and node_modules size.
hints: Note that bun is typically the fastest.

keyTakeaways: npm, pnpm, and bun are compatible with the same package.json format.
pnpm saves disk space with a content-addressable store.
bun is the fastest option — combines package manager and runtime.
Choose based on speed needs, disk constraints and team preference.
lessons.challenge: Set up the same project with all 3 package managers and benchmark install times.

lessons.title: Monorepo Workspace Configurations
lessons.description: Organize multiple related packages in a single repository with shared dependencies and scripts.

sections.heading: What is a monorepo?
paragraphs: A monorepo puts multiple packages or apps in a single repository. Workspaces let them share dependencies and scripts while remaining independent.
list: All packages live in one repo with a root package.json
Workspaces define where packages live: "workspaces": ["packages/*"]
Dependencies are hoisted to the root — saved disk space
Changes across packages are atomic — one commit

codeExamples.heading: Monorepo setup
explanation: The root package.json defines workspaces — where packages live.
Each package has its own package.json and dependencies.
Dependencies are hoisted to the root node_modules for efficiency.
Run scripts across all packages with --workspaces.

practice.task: Create a monorepo with 2 packages: a shared utils library and an app that uses it. Set up workspaces at the root level.

keyTakeaways: Monorepos organize multiple packages in a single repository.
Workspaces define package locations and enable dependency hoisting.
Shared scripts can run across all packages.
Monorepos make cross-package changes atomic and easier to manage.
lessons.challenge: Set up a Turborepo or Nx monorepo with a shared library, a web app and an API server.
